text: Arrays and objects are how JavaScript structures more than one value at a time, and they're exactly the shape real blockchain data arrives in — a block containing a list of transactions, each one a small object of its own. Today covers ordered lists, named properties, nesting them together, and what happens when you reach for a property that isn't there.

An array is an ordered list, like a list of wallet addresses. The first element is always at index 0, not 1 — a detail that trips up every beginner at least once. length tells you how many elements it holds, and push adds one more onto the end without disturbing anything already there.

An object holds named properties instead of numbered positions — a transaction with a from address, a to address, and a value, for example. Dot notation is the common style for reading them; bracket notation does exactly the same thing and is required when the property name is stored in a variable instead of written directly in your code.

Real blockchain data is almost never one flat value — it's an object, like a block, containing an array of its transactions, where each individual transaction is itself its own object. Reading block dot transactions, index zero, dot to, chains property access and array indexing together in one expression, and that exact pattern shows up constantly once this course starts working with real contract data in later chapters.

Accessing a property that doesn't exist on an object doesn't throw an error in JavaScript the way many other languages would — it quietly returns undefined instead. That's forgiving, but it also means a simple typo in a property name fails silently instead of loudly, so it's worth double-checking spelling whenever something unexpectedly reads as undefined.

You're ready for lesson seven when you can read a value two levels deep out of a nested structure, like block dot transactions, index zero, dot to. Arrays for ordered lists, objects for named properties, and nesting them together to match real-world data shapes. Next up: the console and debugging — actually seeing what your code is doing.
